subject: forestSpirit
pitch: A small forest spirit, part deer and part mossy stone. A body of grey river stone covered in soft green moss, slender wooden legs ending in little hooves, branching antlers sprouting tiny white flowers and leaves, a pale wooden mask-like face with two glowing green eyes, and a few fireflies circling its head.

I'm figuring out how to build the body as a faceted stone-like sweep with a procedural paint function that shades moss on upward-facing surfaces, and laying out the skeleton with hips, spine, and leg joints positioned along the deer's length.

I'm reconsidering the hierarchy — maybe it's safer to keep hips as the root joint and have the spine chain start from the same point, mirroring how the SDK examples set up a root joint with a chain beginning at its exact location, like the tail example starting right at the hips point.

Then I'll build a neck chain extending from the chest's last spine joint, using a curved path upward and forward, and attach a head joint at the tip, angled forward and slightly down. For the head itself, I'm picturing a pale wooden mask-like face with glowing green eyes, built using an extrusion of a face outline to give it that spirit-deer skull look.

For the glowing eyes, I'm thinking I could fake a glow effect with a billboard card carrying an SVG radial gradient, though the opacity cutoff might make it look like a hard-edged disc rather than a soft glow -- so simpler bright green eye spheres might be the more reliable choice.

For fireflies, I'm considering small yellow-green spheres scattered around the head, deciding whether to attach them to the root, a body joint like hips, or a dedicated "fireflies" joint so they move naturally with the rig.

For the antlers, I'm sketching branching structures growing from the skull using bezier/catmull curves swept with tapered radii, attached rigidly to the head joint, with secondary tine branches sprouting off points along the main antler curve.

For the neck chain, I'll use a 3-point path with two names so it ends without an extra tip joint, then attach the head joint as a child with its own parent reference and aim point. I'm positioning the head to aim forward and slightly downward from the neck's end.

For head orientation I'll use local word-based offsets (forward/up/left) rather than raw coordinates, since that's more robust against the frame conventions. Then for the legs I'm planning four slender limbs using a limb helper with hip and shoulder joint positions, defining upper leg, lower leg, and hoof segments with specific lengths.

I'm working through leg proportions — picking shoulder/hip heights around 0.82-1.0m, target foot positions near ground level, and adjusting segment lengths so the leg reach matches the vertical distance without being perfectly straight. The chain structure will have three joint points (shoulder, knee, foot) connected by two length segments per leg.

I'm thinking through the bend direction for the front leg's carpal joint versus the hind leg's hock, trying to match real deer anatomy where the knee bulges forward while reasoning about which direction vector to use for a standing pose.

Maybe I should give the hind legs three segments instead—hip, stifle, hock, hoof—to get a more deer-like bend, working out lengths like [0.34, 0.36, 0.2] so the total vertical reach matches the hip height to the ground.

The chain's first joint sits at the hip point with hips as parent, and the role for the whole chain is "leg." For front legs, I'll set the shoulder point and parent it to the spine's chest joint, naming the chain joints shoulder, knee, and hoof.

For sweeping the leg mesh, I'm thinking tubes should taper from thicker near the shoulder to thinner at the foot, using a radius function along the chain. I'll add the hoof as a separate small part attached at the tip joint, maybe a cylinder or cone shape.

For positioning, I'm working out the vertical placement so the hoof's bottom edge sits right at floor level while the leg tube's end meets the hoof's top, aligning everything so the whole leg rests properly on the ground.

I'm settling on materials now—wooden legs in a tan-brown tone with darker brown hooves, and a body resembling grey river stone with moss. For the body I'm thinking of sweeping a chain through the spine with a faceted or boxy cross-section to get that chunky, stone-like silhouette, varying the width and height along the sweep to shape a boulder-like torso roughly 0.3 units wide.

Working out the torso geometry now, placing hip, mid-spine, and chest points slightly above the leg attachment height so the legs plug neatly into the body's underside, and tapering the radius from rear to chest for a rounded-but-faceted stone shape.

For the spine chain, I'm deciding how many joints to use—leaning toward four named points (spine1, spine2, spine3, chest) so I get three proper joints plus a tip joint at the chest, giving the neck a clean parent bone to attach to rather than dangling off an ambiguous midpoint.

I'll place the neck points sloping up and forward from chest toward the head, with a head joint aimed slightly down-forward for the deer's posture. For the face mask, I'm planning to extrude the outline in the plane in front of the head using the head's local frame for positioning.

Since the mask is symmetric, the exact left/right direction doesn't matter much — what matters is getting the thickness axis pointing outward from the face. I'll keep it simple with standard vertical-face axes for the outline orientation.

Thinking about the head tilt though: if the bone aims about 26° downward, a vertical mask oriented straight forward would look slightly mismatched with the head's pitch.
